primary-navigation.what: A row of links, usually across the top of a site or app, that leads to its main sections. It is always visible so people know where they are.
uses: Switching between the main areas of a website or application.
Showing the current section on every page.
Giving first-time visitors a quick overview of what the product offers.
avoid: Many top-level sections that do not fit in one row: use a sidebar or a grouped menu.
Steps of a single task: use a stepper or back and next buttons.
practices: Keep to a handful of clear, short labels.
Mark the current section visibly, not by colour alone.
Use the same links in the same order on every page.
Collapse to a menu on small screens.

utility-navigation.what: A small group of links and buttons, usually at the far end of the header, for account, help, notifications and other tools that are not main sections.
uses: Opening the user account menu or signing out.
Showing notifications and a help link.
Offering search, language or settings shortcuts in the header.
avoid: Main sections of the product: put them in the primary navigation.
Long lists of options: use a menu or a settings page.
practices: Keep it to a few well-known items.
Place it in the same corner on every page.
Give icon-only items a text label for screen readers.
Show a count only when something needs attention.

sidebar-link.what: One link in a vertical navigation list at the side of a page, usually with an icon, a label and sometimes a count of items.
uses: Moving between sections of an app with many areas.
Showing how many items wait in a section, such as unread alerts.
Grouping related pages under a nested link.
avoid: A short list of 2 to 5 sections: top navigation is simpler.
Actions that change data: use a button, not a link.
practices: Write short labels that fit on one line.
Highlight the current page with more than colour.
Make the whole row clickable, not just the text.
Keep icons consistent and always paired with a label.

breadcrumbs.what: A trail of links showing where the current page sits in the site, from the top level down. Each step links back to a higher level.
uses: Helping people find their way in sites with deep levels.
Jumping back up to a parent section in one click.
Showing context on product, document or category pages.
avoid: Sites with only one or two levels: a simple back link is enough.
Showing the steps someone took or a process: use a stepper.
practices: Show the real hierarchy, not the browsing history.
Make the last item the current page and do not link it.
Keep labels short and match page titles.
Place the trail near the top of the page.

pagination.what: Controls that split a long list or set of results into numbered pages, with links to move to the previous, next or a specific page.
uses: Browsing search results or long product lists.
Moving through large tables of data.
Letting people return to a known page of results.
avoid: Short lists that fit on one screen: show everything.
Endless feeds read in one pass: use infinite scroll or a load more button.
practices: Show the current page clearly and mark it for screen readers.
Make links big enough to tap.
Keep the page in the web address so it can be shared.
Use previous and next links as well as numbers.

pagination-summary.what: A line of text that tells people which part of a list they are viewing and how many items there are in total, such as 'Showing 21 to 40 of 312'.
uses: Confirming how many results a search or filter returned.
Orienting people within a long paginated list.
Showing a total next to page controls.
avoid: Lists whose total is unknown or constantly changing: say 'many results' or use load more.
Short lists on one page: a simple count is enough.
practices: Use real numbers and group digits in long numbers.
Update the text as soon as filters change.
Say what the items are, such as videos or orders.
Handle zero results with a clear message.

table-pager.what: A compact set of controls beneath a data table that lets people choose how many rows to show per page and move between pages.
uses: Browsing large data tables in admin screens.
Letting people pick 20, 50 or 100 rows per page.
Showing the range of rows currently displayed.
avoid: Small tables that fit on one screen: show all rows.
Card grids or content lists: use regular pagination or load more.
practices: Put it directly below the table, close to the rows.
Disable previous on the first page and next on the last.
Offer a few sensible page sizes.
Remember the chosen page size between visits.

tab-bar.what: A row of labelled tabs that switches between related views of the same content or object, showing one view at a time.
uses: Splitting a detail page into overview, activity and settings.
Showing different views of the same data in the same space.
Keeping a long page short by grouping content.
avoid: Steps that must happen in order: use a stepper.
Unrelated pages or sections of a site: use navigation links.
practices: Use short, clear labels.
Always show which tab is selected.
Support arrow keys to move between tabs.
Keep the number of tabs small and avoid hiding critical content.

child-tabs.what: Tabs on the page of a parent record, each leading to one kind of related item and showing how many it holds, such as Users (12).
uses: Showing the lists that belong to an account, site or project.
Letting people see at a glance which sections have content.
Navigating between related lists without leaving the parent.
avoid: Views that are not related items of one record: use plain tabs or navigation.
Steps of a process: use a stepper.
practices: Show a count so empty sections are clear before clicking.
Keep the parent summary visible above the tabs.
Order tabs by how often people use them.
Mark the current tab with more than colour.

bottom-navigation.what: A bar fixed to the bottom of a phone screen with three to five main destinations, each shown as an icon with a short label.
uses: Switching between the main areas of a mobile app or site.
Making key destinations easy to reach with a thumb.
Showing a badge for new items on a destination.
avoid: Desktop screens: use a top bar or sidebar.
More than five destinations: use a menu or a navigation drawer.
practices: Pair every icon with a short label.
Mark the current destination clearly.
Keep the same items on every screen.
Leave space for the bar so it does not cover content.

nav-tree.what: A navigation list with collapsible groups, where each group opens to show its links. It organises many destinations into a readable hierarchy.
uses: Navigating large documentation sites or settings areas.
Grouping many pages under named sections.
Showing the user's place inside a deep structure.
avoid: Short lists of links: show them flat.
Deeply nested content with more than three levels: simplify the structure or add search.
practices: Open the group that holds the current page.
Show open and closed state with an icon and text, not colour alone.
Limit nesting to two levels.
Make groups work with the keyboard.

back-link.what: A link that takes people to the previous level or page, usually placed above the page heading, labelled with where it goes.
uses: Returning from a detail page to its list.
Leaving a step in a multi-page form.
Giving phone users a short way back when breadcrumbs do not fit.
avoid: Replacing the browser's back button behaviour: link to a real page instead.
Deep hierarchies where people need many levels: use breadcrumbs.
practices: Name the destination, such as 'Back to orders'.
Place it consistently above the title.
Link to the actual parent page so it works from shared links.
Include a visible arrow as a hint.

view-toggle.what: A small control that lets people switch how the same collection is shown, for example as cards or as a table, without changing the content.
uses: Switching a list between a visual grid and a dense table.
Letting people choose between map and list views.
Matching the view to the task, browsing or comparing.
avoid: Switching between different content: use tabs.
Turning a setting on or off: use a switch or checkbox.
practices: Show all options at once with an icon and a label.
Mark the active view clearly.
Remember the choice for next time.
Keep filters and sorting when the view changes.

settings-toggle.what: A button, usually an icon, that opens or closes a panel of display or app settings without leaving the page.
uses: Opening quick display settings such as theme or density.
Showing options that are used rarely.
Keeping the main screen simple while settings stay close.
avoid: Important settings people need often: show them directly.
Large sets of preferences: use a full settings page.
practices: Use a familiar icon with a text label for assistive tools.
Tell screen readers if the panel is open or closed.
Let Escape close the panel.
Save changes right away and show the result.

create-button.what: The main button for adding a new item, such as a new record or document. It sits near the page title and is the page's primary action.
uses: Adding a new item from a list page.
Starting a new document, report or project.
Keeping the main create action easy to find on every list.
avoid: Pages with several equally important actions: group them in a menu or toolbar.
Actions that change existing items: use a regular button next to the item.
practices: Start the label with a verb and name the item, such as 'Add video'.
Show only one primary create action per page.
Make it easy to reach on phones.
Use an icon only to support the text.

base-layout.what: The basic page skeleton that every page of a site shares: document setup, language, head content, a skip link and places for the page body and scripts.
uses: Making every page start from the same, correct HTML structure.
Setting the language, title and theme once.
Adding shared scripts and styles in one place.
avoid: Pages that need a header, sidebar or footer: extend a layout that includes them.
Small fragments loaded inside a page: return only the fragment.
practices: Set the page language.
Provide a skip link to the main content.
Load shared styles in the head and scripts at the end.
Keep page-specific code out of the shared base.

app-shell.what: The standard frame of a web application: a top bar, a side navigation and a main area for the page title, actions and content.
uses: Building signed-in screens such as lists, forms and dashboards.
Keeping navigation fixed while content changes.
Giving every page the same place for title and actions.
avoid: Public marketing pages: use a simpler site layout with a header and footer.
Sign-in or error pages: use a focused layout without navigation.
practices: Keep navigation in the same place on every page.
Let the sidebar collapse to save space.
Turn the sidebar into a drawer on phones.
Provide a skip link to the main content.

auth-layout.what: A simple, focused page for signing in, creating an account or resetting a password, usually with one centred card and no navigation.
uses: Sign-in and sign-up pages.
Password reset and email confirmation pages.
Invitation or locked-out account pages.
avoid: Pages for signed-in users: use the app layout with navigation.
Long registration with many steps: use a multi-step form layout.
practices: Show one task and remove distractions.
Label every field and show errors next to it.
Allow password managers and show or hide of the password.
Offer a clear link for help or recovery.

email-layout.what: The shared structure of automatic emails such as receipts and password resets: a brand bar, a heading, short text, one main button and a footer.
uses: Sending order confirmations and receipts.
Sending password reset and verification emails.
Sending alerts and notices from an app.
avoid: Newsletters and campaigns with rich design: use a marketing email tool.
Messages that need an immediate response: consider an in-app notice or text message.
practices: Use simple table layouts and inline styles for email apps.
Include a plain-text version.
Print the button's link so it works if the button fails.
Say why the reader got the email.

error-layouts.what: Pages shown when something goes wrong, such as page not found or a server error. They explain what happened and offer a way forward.
uses: Showing a page not found message.
Telling people they lack permission to open a page.
Handling server failures with a calm message.
avoid: Mistakes in a form: show messages next to the fields instead.
Short problems on a part of a page: use an inline message.
practices: Explain what happened in plain words.
Offer a clear next step such as home or search.
Avoid blame and technical jargon.
Keep the page light so it loads even when systems fail.

homepage-template.what: The first page people see after signing in to an app, summarising key numbers, recent activity and shortcuts to common tasks.
uses: Giving a quick status overview of an account or project.
Linking to the tasks people do most.
Showing recent changes since the last visit.
avoid: Marketing landing pages for visitors: use a public site layout.
Detailed analysis: use a dedicated report or dashboard page.
practices: Answer what needs attention first.
Show only a few key figures.
Offer shortcuts to frequent tasks.
Handle new accounts with no data using a helpful empty state.

feed-skeleton.what: A scrolling column of posts or updates that shows grey placeholder shapes while more content loads, and a message when there is nothing yet.
uses: Showing social posts, photo feeds or timelines.
Loading more items as people scroll.
Telling people when a feed is empty.
avoid: Data that people compare in rows and columns: use a table.
Content that people need to jump around in: use pages with navigation.
practices: Match the placeholder shape to the real post.
Keep the column at a readable width.
Avoid layout jumps when real content arrives.
Provide a way to reach the footer or load more with the keyboard.

person-block-grid.what: A grid of cards, one per person, showing a photo or initials, a name, a role and a way to get in touch.
uses: Showing a team or staff page.
Listing members of a project or group.
Building a contact directory.
avoid: Comparing people by several details: use a table.
Long lists that people need to search or sort: use a searchable list.
practices: Use the same card layout for everyone.
Show a name and role next to each photo.
Use initials when there is no photo.
Make contact links clear and large enough to tap.

marketing-layout.what: The frame of public pages that promote a product or service: a header with links and a call to action, wide sections and a footer with link columns.
uses: Building landing, product and pricing pages.
Telling a story in full-width sections.
Guiding visitors to sign up or contact sales.
avoid: Signed-in application screens: use an app layout.
Long reading content: use an article or documentation layout.
practices: Offer one clear main call to action per screen.
Keep the header simple and familiar.
Use generous spacing and short sections.
Put key links and legal information in the footer.

blog-layout.what: A page designed for reading long text, with a title, an introduction, sections in a comfortable column and a contents list to jump between them.
uses: Articles, guides and release notes.
Case studies and policies.
Any page that is mostly sections of text.
avoid: Short pages of mostly interface: use a standard page layout.
Data-heavy pages: use a dashboard or table layout.
practices: Keep lines to about 60 to 75 characters.
Open with a short summary.
Use clear headings that match the contents list.
Show the publish or update date.

docs-layout.what: A page layout for documentation, with a navigation tree on the left, the article in the middle and a list of sections on the right.
uses: Product documentation and help centres.
Internal handbooks and wikis.
API or developer guides.
avoid: Marketing pages: use a public site layout.
A single short article: a simple reading layout is enough.
practices: Group pages in clear, named sections.
Provide search or a filter for navigation.
Highlight the current page in the tree.
Show versions and last updated dates.

button.what: A control that triggers an action when pressed, such as saving a form or opening a dialog. Its style shows how important the action is.
uses: Submitting forms and saving changes.
Opening dialogs and starting actions.
Confirming or cancelling a decision.
avoid: Moving to another page: use a link.
Several equally strong buttons on one screen: pick one primary action.
practices: Start labels with a verb and name the result, such as 'Save image'.
Use one primary button per screen.
Make buttons at least 44 pixels tall on touch screens.
Show a busy state during slow actions.
Show disabled state with a clear reason.

button-size.what: Different heights and widths for buttons, such as small, regular and large, chosen to fit the place and the device where they appear.
uses: Using compact buttons in tables and toolbars.
Using large buttons for touch screens and main phone actions.
Making a full-width button at the bottom of a form.
avoid: Showing importance: change the button style, not its size.
Mixing many sizes in one row: choose one size for the group.
practices: Keep the same size for buttons in a row.
Make touch targets at least 44 pixels.
Match button height to nearby fields.
Add an accessible name to icon-only buttons.

link-action.what: A button or link drawn as plain text for low-priority actions, such as 'Clear filters' or 'Show more', that should not compete with main buttons.
uses: Clearing filters or resetting a form.
Showing more or less content.
Linking to related pages within a sentence.
avoid: The main action of a screen: use a primary button.
Actions that need strong emphasis, such as deleting: use a button with clear styling.
practices: Underline or style it so it looks clickable.
Name the result, never 'click here'.
Use a real link for navigation and a button for actions.
Keep the text short.

pin-button.what: A toggle button that pins an item so it stays at the top of a list or on a dashboard. Pressing it again removes the pin.
uses: Keeping favourite items at the top of a list.
Adding a report or album to a dashboard.
Marking items for quick access.
avoid: Marking a one-off choice for a bulk action: use a checkbox.
Rating or liking content: use a star or heart control.
practices: Show pinned and unpinned states clearly.
Name the item in the accessible label, such as 'Pin Entrance A'.
Save the state on the server.
Update the label when the state changes.

email-button.what: A link that opens the user's email app with the recipient, subject and body filled in, styled as a button.
uses: Contacting support or sales.
Sending a link or report by email.
Replying to an alert or notice.
avoid: Forms that collect detailed messages: use a contact form.
Users without a mail app: always show the address as well.
practices: Show the email address beside the button.
Set a helpful subject line.
Encode special characters in the link.
Label it with what will happen, such as 'Email support'.

toggle-button.what: A button that stays pressed to show something is on and pops back when pressed again, used to switch a mode or a display option.
uses: Turning toolbar options on or off, such as grid lines or bold.
Switching a live view or mute on and off.
Filtering a list with an on-off chip.
avoid: Settings that are saved and applied later: use a switch.
Choosing one option from several: use radio buttons or a segmented control.
practices: Keep the label the same in both states.
Show the pressed state with more than colour.
Tell assistive tools the pressed state.
Make the change take effect right away.

icon-button.what: A button that shows only an icon, used for common actions such as close, search or more options, when space is limited.
uses: Closing dialogs and panels.
Providing toolbar actions such as refresh or edit.
Opening an overflow menu.
avoid: Actions with an unfamiliar icon: use a text button.
Destructive actions without confirmation: add a confirm step.
practices: Give every icon button an accessible name.
Use widely known icons.
Make the target at least 44 pixels on touch.
Add a tooltip when the meaning may be unclear.

fab.what: A large round or pill-shaped button that floats above the page, usually at the bottom right of a phone screen, for the main action.
uses: Creating a new item on a mobile list screen.
Starting the main task of a mobile app.
Keeping the primary action in reach while scrolling.
avoid: Desktop screens: put the main action in the page header.
Screens with several equal actions: use a regular toolbar.
practices: Use it for one primary action only.
Prefer an icon with a text label.
Leave space so it does not cover content.
Give icon-only versions an accessible name.

icon.what: A small picture that stands for an object or action, such as a magnifier for search. Icons help people recognise things quickly.
uses: Adding meaning next to labels in buttons and menus.
Marking status in messages and lists.
Saving space in toolbars with well-known symbols.
avoid: Ideas without a well-known symbol: use words.
Decoration that competes with the content.
practices: Pair icons with text whenever possible.
Use one style and line weight throughout.
Give standalone icons an accessible name.
Let icons inherit the colour of the text.

status-icon.what: A symbol that shows state, such as success, warning, error or information. Each has its own shape and colour so it can be told apart.
uses: Showing results in alerts and messages.
Marking errors next to form fields.
Showing the state of a job, device or item.
avoid: Pure decoration: choose a neutral icon or none.
Long explanations: use a text message.
practices: Use different shapes, not only different colours.
Always add a word with the icon.
Use the same icon for the same meaning everywhere.
Keep colours with enough contrast.

icon-set.what: The collection of icons a product draws from, all sharing one size grid, line weight and style so the interface looks consistent.
uses: Choosing a symbol for a new button or menu item.
Keeping the look of icons consistent across screens.
Finding standard names for common concepts.
avoid: Mixing icons from several sets on one screen.
Inventing new symbols for well-known actions: use the familiar one.
practices: Pick icons that match the word, such as a bin for delete.
Keep the same size and weight.
Do not use one icon for two meanings.
Add new icons in the same style.

capture-run-progress.what: A view of a long-running job, such as an export, that shows overall progress, the current step, time left and the result for each item.
uses: Following exports, imports and bulk updates.
Showing which items finished or failed.
Letting people cancel or retry a job.
avoid: Quick actions under about 10 seconds: a simple spinner is enough.
Jobs that run in the background for hours: send a notification when done.
practices: Show progress, the current step and an estimate.
Tell screen readers about updates politely.
Update at a calm pace, not every frame.
End with a clear summary and a way to retry failures.
